case_prompt:
A 27-year-old White man presented with a 2-year history of episodic fevers and tender erythematous rash predominantly on his trunk. Flares were preceded by prodromal flu-like symptoms, low-grade fever, sore throat, and arthralgias; during these episodes he also reported intermittent diarrhea and severe headache. Each flare lasted 3 to 7 days and recurred approximately every 3 weeks, at times rendering him bedbound. He had a history only of seasonal allergic rhinitis and no family history of autoimmune disease.  

Biopsies of the rash demonstrated a perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate without evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis. The patient had trialed multiple antihistamines, oral prednisone, and monthly omalizumab injections without improvement. Further laboratory evaluation showed mildly decreased C4 (12.8 mg/mL), normal C3, negative antinuclear antibodies, negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, negative rheumatoid factor, normal thyroid hormones, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, negative celiac serologies, normal serum IgA, serotonin, chromogranin A, and tryptase levels, negative hepatitis, HIV, toxocara, and tuberculosis screening, normal urinary catecholamines, metanephrines, 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, and a normal chronic urticaria index (while receiving omalizumab).  

Because of his gastrointestinal symptoms, a colonoscopy was performed and showed no evidence of inflammatory bowel disease.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Urticarial vasculitis considered and excluded — “demonstrated perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate with no evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.” 2. Chronic spontaneous urticaria considered and excluded — “The chronic urticaria index was within normal limits.” and “patient trialed multiple antihistamines … and monthly omalizumab … with no relief.” 3. Crohn’s disease considered and excluded — “A colonoscopy was performed with no evidence of inflammatory bowel disease.” 4. Blau syndrome considered and excluded — “BS is primarily a pediatric disease characterized by a triad of granulomatous dermatitis, uveitis, and inflammatory arthritis. Development of disease in adults and the presence of fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea are rarely seen.”

selection.screen_reason: Recurrent 3-7 day fevers with dermatitis, arthralgia and diarrhea after an extensive negative workup fit Yao syndrome; NOD2 genotyping is the orderable confirmation.
selection.second_look_note: Two years of stereotyped 3-7 day flares of fever, rash, arthralgia, sore throat and diarrhea every 3 weeks with an extensive negative workup fit Yao syndrome.
